Junpeng Lao

  • 3rd+

Chief Epistemologist at rekursiv.ai

2w • Edited • 


Follow
Multi-agent workflows are all the rage. But
advancing science takes more than throwing
10,000 agents at a problem.

Over three days and 6,164 experiments, we at
@rekursiv.ai reached a new state of the art on
Andrej Karpathy's NanoChat benchmark:
📊 0.88982 mean BPB across 10 seeds (a 1.3%
improvement over the previous best).

Reaching that score required more than raw
compute. We had to improve how the research team
itself worked: Enter 🟢 meta-harness 🟢 

What happens when your AI scientist finishes an
experiment, but the colleague waiting for its result
no longer exists?
An AI reviewer caught that exact failure in our
NanoChat campaign: engineer agents tried
returning results to researcher sessions that had
already closed. The coordinator adapted, routing
late results through a supervisor and durable
records.

That feedback loop is where automated science gets
interesting. Along the way, we were debugging the
research team itself:
• Who checks the evidence before accepting a run?
• How do results reach the next scientist?
• What happens when an asynchronous handoff
breaks?

To connect hypotheses, experiments, and evidence,
we built and used Trackinizer
(https://lnkd.in/eMDS3F-c). When agents asked,
“What should we test next, and what would make
us change our mind?”, both humans and models
could inspect the chain of evidence and steer the
next run.

6,164 experiments. NanoChat SoTA. And a research
process that learns from its failures.

If you are building research agents, which handoffs
keep breaking in your setup?

🔗 Read the full story: https://lnkd.in/e3gChbpe
🧪 Try the recipe: https://lnkd.in/e5m4U8am
💬 Join our Discord: https://lnkd.in/ez4SQyMx


Additional:
We sent a swarm of AI agents to solve Karpathy’s
NanoChat benchmark, and they crushed SoTA in 3
days.

We built our own harness on top of a graph database
to do auto-autoresearch, each iteration learning
from mistakes to do research better.
The team wrote >15,000 entries.

post_text:
Recently I have been trying to figure out how much
of the evals process can be "automated" with AI.
Surely we should be able to automate a lot; AI has
gotten so good. Unfortunately you can't fully
automate your evals! 

Plenty of vendors will sell you the opposite. Point
their LLM-powered tool at your agent traces, and
it'll tell you where your application is broken and fix
it for you. I would love for this to be true.

These tools can find some errors. But they cannot
find all! For one reason, what "good" means for your
product lives in your head. It’s not in the traces.
Anything you haven't externalized, into the traces
or the prompt, the agent will never find. 
Moreover, if a tool could fully build and fix your
product for you, it could do the same for everyone
else, all of your competitors. There would be nothing
left to set your product apart. Your judgment is the
only differentiating factor you have.

So the question becomes: what can AI do for evals, if
it can't do them end-to-end? It can accelerate your
review of your traces! It can
- Build a custom UI for you to review your traces
- Intelligently cluster and sample which traces to
use
- Take some of your annotations or labeled failures,
reflect on them, and try to find other traces that the
same annotations would apply to

My general rule of thumb is: I've found it's far
easier to say what I think and have the agent scale
that out across many traces than to sit and validate
the agent's taste (i.e., have the agent do error
analysis from scratch). 

Learning to do this, finding what's broken and
knowing what counts as a mistake, is the core of
what Hamel and I teach in our AI Evals course. If
you want to go deeper on evals, the final cohort of
the year starts Oct 10: https://lnkd.in/gfp5gvBW
observed_comment:
I think the label needs to carry more than the failure
type. It should also record which decision was
affected, who owns it, and what recovery costs. 

Otherwise AI can scale the taxonomy without
helping the team decide which failures matter first.

post_text:
While building Braintrust I’ve been thinking about
what evals are good at, what they should be used
for, and how they differ from other parts of the
software development lifecycle, like tests.

Though it’s tempting to conflate evals and tests,
doing so confuses the differences between them.

Here’s how we think about it at Braintrust:
- A test is about if the thing can work
- An eval is about what the thing can and cannot do
- A mature eval practice is about what the thing
should be doing, how often, and in what
circumstances

The last one is important when building agents. You
need to test that something is working, measure
what it’s capable of, then take this data and use it to
build new behaviors for your agent.

In traditional software you use tests to understand
correctness and observability to understand
performance. Correctness captures whether or not
your software can work as expected, and
performance measures how well your software does
that work in the real world.

For agents, correctness also requires information
about how the agent works. Is it calling the right
tools? Is it surfacing the right information?

This is how you measure if an agent is working, and
tests still have their place here. You shouldn’t
replace an eval with a test, but you shouldn’t stop
testing altogether either.

But what if the way the agent works needs to
change? Or what if you want to use system data to
inform how it should change?

All of this goes beyond the capabilities of a test.
What you want to know is what an agent is capable
of, and whether this behavior is correct in novel
situations. This is why evals exist.

As agents have grown in complexity and power this
has become critical. A mature eval suite should tell
you what the thing can do, and document what it
does when it is exhibiting new behavior. Then you
can use that data to determine what it should be
doing, so you can improve the quality of the agent as
these new behaviors emerge.

With this in mind, you can see why evals and tests
are separate things, both of which have their place.

A healthy eval practice means that each time a user
encounters unexpected behavior, teams can save it
in a dataset and add it to their eval suite.

A healthy testing practice means that as you update
the implementation of an agent based on those
evals, you can write tests that assert it's working
well.

At Braintrust we’re focused on the evals. We want
our customers to observe agent behavior, turn those
traces into evals, and build the continuous loop of
agent improvement. We envision a world of active
observability, in which this eval practice supports
the automatic surfacing of issues before a team
knows to look for them.

If you're interested in building evals, Braintrust can
help: https://lnkd.in/gRv7ASXF

Uku Joost Annus Raises €615K to Scale AI-Powered
Mobile App Building

Estonian startup bilt.me has raised €614,900
($700,000) in pre-seed funding to expand its AI-
native platform that lets users turn an idea into a
working mobile application. The round was led by
Superhero Capital, with participation from Bolt
founder Markus Villig and Lightyear founder
Martin Sokk.

Founded in August 2025 by Uku Joost Annus, Kevin
Akkermann and Karl Kiilaspää, bilt.me began as a
hackathon project in Tallinn before evolving into a
platform focused specifically on native mobile
applications.

Its AI agent allows users to describe an app in plain
language, generate a native iOS or Android
application, preview it on a phone and work toward
publishing it on the App Store or Google Play. The
platform also includes payments, cloud
infrastructure and app-sharing capabilities, while
allowing users to export React Native code.

The early traction is notable: bilt.me says thousands
of people are already building on the platform,
while revenue has surpassed six figures in annual
recurring revenue and doubled month over month
for three consecutive months. The company plans to
use the new capital for global expansion and further
product development.

The bigger shift: AI is moving from helping
developers write code to taking users from an idea
to a published mobile product.

post_text:
"How do you get ideas for posts?"

People ask me this a lot, here's how:

1. I have a doc where I store ideas throughout the
day/week, not full drafts, just a quick note on the
idea for the specific post (notes app is another great
spot to jot down ideas).

2. I take lots of pictures, especially for LinkedIn this
is helpful since they seem to boost posts with
photos. I get a lot of my post ideas from scrolling
through my camera roll and building a post off of a
recent experience (that I have a photo of).

3. pull from different buckets. Personal life, work
life, humor, learnings, experiences/stories, hot
takes/beliefs, etc. etc. 

4. start small. If you have a full time job, you
probably don't have an hour/day to write a
LinkedIn post (which is how long it used to take me
when I was getting started). I started with posting
3 times a week and eventually ramped it up to more.

5. be consistent, there's a lot of different opinions
about how many times a week you should post. I
don't think it matters that much, whether it's 1 time
or 5 times a week, pick a number and commit to it. 

6. follow cool people, I get a lot of inspiration for
posts from seeing what other people are doing on
here.


This is what I've picked up from posting
consistently on here for the past year (ish).

At the end of the day, there's pretty much zero
downside and unlimited upside to posting on here,
it's dramatically changed my life in the short year
that I've been doing it.

"Anyone can cook (and post on LinkedIn), but only
the fearless can be great" - Chef Gusteau


(picture I randomly took of my laptop in starbucks
before I shipped my first LinkedIn post lol)
